# Maps of Content

A Map of Content (MOC, said "EM-OH-CEE") is a note made mainly of links that maps a cluster of related notes in context. It is Nick Milo's central thinking tool and the best-known higher-order note. Informally MOCs are called "maps".

## When to make one
According to Milo, build a MOC when you feel the tickle of overwhelm described in Mental Squeeze Point (LYT), for example when 20 scattered notes belong to one effort. Placing their links in a new MOC is like laying 20 index cards on a workbench. You never have to tend a MOC: it can sit untouched for a year and still be useful.

## The three phases
The phases overlap and are non-linear; Milo calls the cycle a coda, where the tail meets the head.
1. **Gather**: collect, curate and incubate related notes on a "workbench". Only links are assembled; nothing is organized yet.
2. **Develop (collide)**: ideas compete for relational position. Questions arise naturally: what are these notes saying, what is redundant, what should be split, which outside concepts relate? In Milo's habits walkthrough this produced new Evergreen Notes (LYT), including splitting an over-large note into two. He calls this the most joyful and valuable phase.
3. **Navigate**: connect the finished map to the rest of the network and structure it for future use, as a reference, as a basis for outputs, or for the pleasure of the ideas. The MOC remains a renewable summary for Future You.

A MOC is rarely a finished statue. Adding stray notes to a formalized MOC is encouraged, and starting a fresh MOC is also fine.

## Why MOCs help
Milo's list: they manage anxiety, create a concentrated space for idea interaction, become a reference that can leave a new project largely complete, stay as reliable navigation and memory aids, evolve with your thinking, and stay non-destructive. They are overlays rather than containers, so one set of notes can be mapped in different ways (heterarchy rather than hierarchy). In the kit the same 19 concepts are regrouped by strategy, improvement or weight to show this.

## MOC versus other forms
- **Index or table of contents**: a MOC can act as a static index, but its power is gathering, developing, colliding and refactoring ideas. A table of contents has one fixed linear order and is usually tied to a project. Milo often sees a MOC and a table of contents working together: the MOC is the broad worktable, the table of contents the final structure.
- **Folders**: folders limit access; MOCs curate it.

## Linking upward
Milo links each note up to a map, and the map up to the Home Note, so any note is a few clicks from home. A contextual "unrequited notes" query (notes that link to the map but are not linked back) is his preferred way to surface missing connections.

> [!contradiction] Phase naming
> The walkthrough calls the middle phase "Collide"; the FAQ and glossary say "develop". They are treated as the same phase here.
